title: Elements: the 118 kinds of atom, metals and non-metals, and the elements in your body

summary.text: Sugar and salt are both white grains, yet on a hot tawa sugar turns black and salt stays white. The black is carbon, an element that was inside the white sugar all the time. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom, and 118 elements are known. Most of them are metals, but your body is built almost entirely from four non-metals: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen. Your child heats eight kitchen things to find which ones hold carbon. They colour a hundred square of the elements in their own body. They also test whether pencil lead, which is carbon, passes the tests for a metal.
summary.art: An old tawa covered with foil, with a small black heap where sugar was and a small white heap of salt beside it, and a girl of nine looking closely from an arm's length away.

intro.hook: Sugar is white. Salt is white. A grown-up heats a pinch of each on a tawa, and one of them turns black. Which one, and where did the black come from?
intro.text: The black is an element called carbon. It was inside the sugar before the heating, joined with two other elements. There is carbon in rice, in cotton, in paper and in you. In this unit you find out which kitchen things hold carbon. You colour the elements of your own body on a hundred square. You number all 118 elements on a grid and see how many are metals. You also put pencil lead through three tests for a metal.
intro.art: Two small white heaps side by side on a steel plate, one labelled sugar and one labelled salt, with a question mark drawn above them.

outcomes: I can say what an element is, that 118 are known, and that about 90 are found in nature.
I can read common element symbols, and say why Na, K and Fe do not match the English names.
I can name the properties most metals share, and test things for them.
I can say how non-metals differ from metals, and name non-metals that are gases, liquids and solids.
I can explain why some elements, such as carbon and silicon, do not fit neatly on either side.
I can name the main elements in my body and say how much of my weight each one is.
I can explain why counting by weight and counting atoms give different answers about my body.
I can test which things hold carbon, and say what I thought, what I saw and why.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see.
terms.example: A grain of sugar holds more atoms than there are grains of sand on a beach.
terms.art: A grain of sugar with a zoom circle showing many tiny balls packed together.

terms.meaning: A substance made of only one kind of atom.
terms.example: Pure gold has only gold atoms. Oxygen gas has only oxygen atoms.
terms.art: A gold bangle with a zoom circle showing identical yellow balls.

terms.meaning: A substance made of two or more elements joined together.
terms.example: Water is hydrogen joined with oxygen. Sugar is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen joined together.
terms.art: A drop of water with a zoom circle showing one large ball joined to two small balls.

terms.meaning: The number that each element has, from 1 to 118. It counts the protons, which are particles in the centre of the atom.
terms.example: Hydrogen is number 1. Carbon is number 6. Gold is number 79.
terms.art: A row of numbered boxes from 1 to 8, with box 6 marked C.

terms.meaning: The one or two letters that scientists everywhere use for an element.
terms.example: O is oxygen, C is carbon, and Na is sodium.
terms.art: Three cards showing the letters O, C and Na.

terms.meaning: An element that is usually shiny, bends without breaking, and carries heat and electricity well.
terms.example: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver are metals.
terms.art: A steel tumbler, a copper wire and a gold ring side by side.

terms.meaning: An element that lacks most of the properties of metals. Many non-metals are gases, and the solid ones are usually brittle.
terms.example: Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon and sulfur are non-metals.
terms.art: A balloon labelled oxygen beside a lump of charcoal and a yellow lump of sulfur.

terms.meaning: An element with some properties of a metal and some of a non-metal.
terms.example: Silicon is shiny like a metal but breaks like glass. It is used in the chips inside phones.
terms.art: A shiny grey lump of silicon beside a tiny computer chip.

terms.meaning: The shine of a clean metal surface.
terms.example: A steel plate shines again when you scrub it.
terms.art: A steel plate, half dull and half scrubbed bright.

terms.meaning: Able to be beaten or pressed into a new shape without breaking.
terms.example: Silver is beaten into the thin leaf, called varak, that covers some sweets.
terms.art: A hammer flattening a small ball of metal into a thin sheet.

terms.meaning: Breaking or crumbling when it is hit or bent.
terms.example: Pencil lead and charcoal are brittle. They snap and do not bend.
terms.art: A pencil lead snapped into two pieces.

terms.meaning: A material that lets heat or electricity pass through it easily.
terms.example: Copper is a good conductor, so electric wires are made of copper.
terms.art: A cut electric cable showing bright copper wires inside plastic.

terms.meaning: A non-metal element, number 6. Every living thing is built around carbon atoms.
terms.example: Charcoal, pencil lead and diamond are carbon. The black on burnt toast is mostly carbon.
terms.art: A piece of charcoal, a pencil and a diamond in a row.

terms.meaning: An element that the body needs in a very small amount.
terms.example: Your body holds only a few grams of iron, but your blood needs it to carry oxygen.

explanations.concept: An element is one kind of atom
explanations.definition: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into anything simpler by heating or by mixing.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, which are particles far too small to see. There are different kinds of atom. A substance with only one kind is called an element. Gold is an element, because every atom in pure gold is a gold atom. Water is a compound, because it is hydrogen atoms joined with oxygen atoms. Sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. A compound can look nothing like the elements in it. Sugar is white and sweet. The carbon in it is black, and the hydrogen and oxygen are gases with no colour. Most things around you are compounds or mixtures. Only a few things at home are nearly pure elements.
examples: The aluminium in kitchen foil is an element.
The copper inside an electric wire is an element.
Salt is a compound of two elements, sodium and chlorine.
explanations.art: A sugar crystal with a zoom circle showing black, white and red balls joined in a group.

explanations.definition: Scientists know 118 elements. Each has an atomic number from 1 to 118, which counts the protons in the centre of its atom.
explanations.description: The centre of an atom holds particles called protons. Hydrogen has 1 proton, so it is element number 1. Carbon has 6, and oxygen has 8. An atom with 79 protons is always gold. There is no element with 6 and a half protons, so there are no gaps in the list. About 90 of the 118 elements are found in nature on the Earth. People made the rest in laboratories, by smashing lighter atoms together. Many of those last less than one second before they break apart. The newest four were named in 2016. Number 118 is oganesson, and only a few atoms of it have ever been made. Nobody knows yet whether more elements can be made.
examples: Hydrogen is number 1, the lightest element.
Uranium is number 92, the heaviest element found in large amounts in nature.
Oganesson is number 118. Its atoms last about a thousandth of a second.
explanations.art: A long strip of 118 small numbered squares, with square 1, square 6, square 8, square 79 and square 118 picked out in colour.

explanations.definition: A symbol is one or two letters that stand for an element. The first letter is a capital and the second is small.
explanations.description: People speak thousands of languages, but all scientists use the same symbols. Many symbols are the first letters of the English name. H is hydrogen, C is carbon, and Ca is calcium. Some come from the old Latin name. Sodium is Na, from natrium. Potassium is K, from kalium. Iron is Fe, from ferrum. Gold is Au, from aurum, and silver is Ag, from argentum. The symbols let a chemist in Chennai read the work of a chemist in Japan. You can find symbols on labels at home. A packet of fertiliser marked NPK holds nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
examples: O is oxygen and N is nitrogen.
Fe is iron. The word 'ferrous' on iron tablets comes from ferrum, the Latin name for iron.
Hg is mercury, from a Latin name that means liquid silver.
explanations.art: Six cards in two rows, showing H, C, O above and Na, K, Fe below.

explanations.definition: Most metals shine when clean, bend or flatten without breaking, ring when struck, and carry heat and electricity well.
explanations.description: Metals behave alike because of their atoms. In a metal, some electrons are free to move from atom to atom. An electron is a very light particle that carries electricity. These moving electrons carry electricity along a wire. They also pass heat on quickly, so a steel spoon in hot rasam soon feels hot. They throw light back, which gives a clean metal its shine, called lustre. The atoms of a metal can slide past each other and still hold together. So a metal can be beaten into a sheet, which is called being malleable. It can also be pulled into a wire. A struck metal shakes for a long time, so it rings. Not every metal has every property. Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Sodium is so soft that a knife cuts it.
examples: One gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet nearly one square metre in size.
Temple bells and ghungroos are made of metal because metal rings.
Aluminium is rolled into foil thinner than a hair.
explanations.art: A copper wire, a sheet of foil, a temple bell and a shining steel plate, each with a one-word label: wire, sheet, ring, shine.

explanations.definition: Non-metals are the elements that lack most of the properties of metals. Only 17 of the elements are non-metals.
explanations.description: Eleven non-metals are gases at room temperature. Oxygen and nitrogen make up almost all of the air. Helium, neon and argon are gases too. One non-metal, bromine, is a liquid. The rest, such as carbon, sulfur, phosphorus and iodine, are solids. A solid non-metal is usually brittle, which means it snaps or crumbles when you hit it. Most non-metals are poor conductors of heat and electricity. They do not ring. There are few non-metals, but they matter a great deal. The air, the water and almost all of every living body are made of non-metals.
examples: Air is about 78 parts nitrogen and 21 parts oxygen in every 100.
The brown striking strip on the side of a matchbox holds phosphorus.
The gas inside many light bulbs and tube lights is argon.
explanations.art: A row of four things: a balloon, a lump of charcoal, a yellow lump of sulfur and a matchbox with its striking strip marked.

explanations.concept: Where is the line between metals and non-metals?
explanations.description: Some elements do not sit clearly on one side. Six elements, such as silicon, are called metalloids. Silicon shines like a metal but shatters like glass, and it carries a little electricity. Carbon is a non-metal, yet one form of it behaves partly like a metal. Pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon. Graphite is shiny and carries electricity, but it snaps when you bend it. Diamond is also pure carbon, and it carries no electricity at all. The atoms are the same, and only their arrangement differs. Hydrogen is a non-metal gas on the Earth. Deep inside the planet Jupiter it is squeezed so hard that it behaves as a liquid metal.
examples: Graphite carries electricity, and diamond does not. Both are carbon.
Silicon is used in computer chips because it carries electricity only a little.
Tin is a metal, but in great cold it slowly crumbles to a grey powder.

perspectives.explanation: Sort each element by how it behaves in an ordinary room. Then carbon is a non-metal and iron is a metal. A few elements in between are called metalloids.
A substance is a metal whenever some of its electrons are free to move. That depends on how the atoms are arranged and how hard they are squeezed. So 'metal' describes a state that an element is in.

explanations.art: A pencil lead and a diamond side by side, each with a zoom circle: flat sheets of balls for the pencil lead and a tight three-way frame of balls for the diamond.

explanations.concept: The elements in your body, by weight
explanations.definition: In every 100 parts of a human body's weight, about 65 are oxygen, 18 carbon, 10 hydrogen and 3 nitrogen.
explanations.description: Six elements make up 99 parts in every 100 of your weight. They are oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus. Oxygen comes first because more than half of your body is water. Most of the weight of water is oxygen. Carbon is the frame of fat, protein and sugar. Nitrogen is in every protein. Calcium and phosphorus make your bones and teeth hard. The last 1 part holds about 20 more elements. Sodium and potassium help nerves carry signals. Iron in the blood carries oxygen. Iodine is needed by a gland in the neck, which is why salt is iodised. Almost none of these elements are loose in your body. They are joined into compounds such as water, protein and bone.
examples: A child of 30 kilograms holds about 19 and a half kilograms of oxygen.
A grown-up holds about 1 kilogram of calcium, nearly all of it in bones and teeth.
A grown-up holds only 3 to 4 grams of iron, about the weight of a small nail.
explanations.art: An outline of a child filled with a hundred small squares in bands of colour, the largest band labelled oxygen.

explanations.definition: If you count the atoms in a body one by one, hydrogen comes first. About 62 of every 100 atoms in you are hydrogen.
explanations.description: Atoms of different elements have different weights. An oxygen atom weighs about 16 times as much as a hydrogen atom. A carbon atom weighs about 12 times as much. Water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. So two of every three atoms in water are hydrogen. But the one oxygen atom holds eight ninths of the weight. Your body is the same. Count the atoms, and about 62 in every 100 are hydrogen, 24 are oxygen and 12 are carbon. Weigh them, and oxygen is 65 parts in every 100. Both counts are correct. They answer two different questions: which atoms are most common, and which atoms carry most weight.
examples: In water, hydrogen makes up 2 of every 3 atoms. Yet hydrogen is only 1 ninth of the weight of the water.
In your body, 62 of every 100 atoms are hydrogen. Yet hydrogen is only 10 parts in every 100 of your weight.

Think of a lorry and three cycles on a road. There are more cycles than lorries, so the cycles win if you count. The lorry weighs far more than the three cycles together, so the lorry wins if you weigh.
explanations.art: A balance with one large ball marked O on one pan and sixteen small balls marked H on the other pan, level.

explanations.concept: Carbon, the element living things are built around
explanations.definition: Every living thing is made of compounds built around chains and rings of carbon atoms.
explanations.description: A carbon atom can join to four other atoms at once, and carbon atoms join easily to each other. So carbon makes long chains and rings. Sugar, fat, protein, wood, cotton and paper are all carbon chains with hydrogen and oxygen attached. Strong heat breaks these compounds. The hydrogen and oxygen leave as water vapour and other gases. Much of the carbon stays behind as a black solid. That is why sugar, rice, bread and cotton all turn black on a hot tawa. Salt holds no carbon, so it stays white. A few things hold carbon that does not show as black. Chalk and cooking soda hold carbon joined tightly to oxygen, and they stay white when heated.
examples: A burnt dosa edge is black because the carbon of the batter is left behind.
Charcoal is wood that was heated with very little air, so mostly carbon remains.
Salt and a steel pin on the same hot tawa do not turn black.
explanations.art: Six small heaps on foil, five of them black and one white, with labels sugar, rice, bread, cotton, paper and salt.

explanations.definition: Hydrogen was made soon after the universe began. Almost all other elements were made later inside stars or when stars exploded or collided.
explanations.description: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. In its first few minutes it made hydrogen, helium and a tiny amount of lithium. Stars formed later from this gas. Deep inside a star, hydrogen atoms are pressed together to make helium, and this gives out the star's light. Older stars press helium into carbon and oxygen. Very large stars build elements up to iron and then explode. The explosion scatters these elements into space. Elements heavier than iron, such as gold, are made in such explosions and when two dead stars collide. The Sun, the Earth and your body formed from this scattered matter. Margaret Burbidge and three other scientists worked this out in 1957. Today hydrogen and helium are still about 98 parts in every 100 of the ordinary matter in the universe.
examples: Every hydrogen atom in your body is about 13.8 billion years old.
The calcium in your teeth was made inside large stars.
In 2017 astronomers watched two dead stars collide and saw the light of freshly made heavy elements.
explanations.art: A star throwing out a cloud of glowing gas, with an arrow from the cloud to a small Earth and a child standing on it.

agreed.text: Everything we can touch is made from the same list of elements, and 118 are known.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have taken apart thousands of substances from rocks, air, sea and living bodies. They always reach the same elements, each with its own atomic number.

agreed.text: A compound can look and behave nothing like the elements in it.
agreed.evidence: Sugar is white and sweet. Strong heat drives off water vapour and leaves black carbon, as in the Black Test.

agreed.text: A living body is made of ordinary elements. No element is found only in living things.
agreed.evidence: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound found in urine. He made it from substances that had never been in a living body.

agreed.text: Most elements are metals, but living bodies are almost all non-metal.
agreed.evidence: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen are non-metals. Together they make up 96 parts in every 100 of a human body by weight.

agreed.text: The Sun and the stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
agreed.evidence: In 1925 Cecilia Payne studied the colours missing from starlight. She showed that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium. Other astronomers doubted her at first, and later agreed.

agreed.text: Elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were built inside stars.
agreed.evidence: In 1957 Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed how stars build each element. The amounts they worked out match what astronomers measure.

challenging.claim: The elements are earth, water, air, fire and space.
challenging.who: Many old traditions. In India they are called the pancha bhuta. Greek thinkers listed four of them.
challenging.for: It was the first clear idea that everything is made from a few basic kinds. The five also match solid, liquid, gas, energy and space quite well.
challenging.against: Water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen, and air is a mixture of gases. So neither is an element in the chemist's meaning. The idea of a short list was right, and the list was wrong.

challenging.claim: All metals are hard, heavy solids.
challenging.for: Iron, copper and steel are hard and heavy, and they are the metals we meet most.
challenging.against: Mercury is a liquid. Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife, and it is lighter than water. The metal gallium melts in a warm hand.

challenging.who: A common belief, and a useful first rule.
challenging.for: Wires are metal, and most non-metals such as wood, rubber and sulfur carry almost none.
challenging.against: Graphite is carbon, a non-metal, and it carries electricity. Salt water carries electricity too.

challenging.claim: Living bodies are made of a special living matter that is different from the matter of rocks.
challenging.who: Many scientists before the 1800s. The idea is called vitalism.
challenging.for: Living things grow, heal and have young, and rocks do not seem to.
challenging.against: Wöhler made urea in 1828 from non-living substances. Every element in a body is also found in rocks, air or sea.

challenging.who: Physicists, since Eugene Wigner and Hillard Huntington suggested it in 1935.
challenging.for: Measurements of Jupiter fit a deep layer of liquid hydrogen that carries electricity as a metal does.
challenging.against: On the Earth, making solid metallic hydrogen needs enormous pressure. A claim to have made it in 2017 has not been repeated by others.

challenging.claim: There can be no more than 118 elements.
challenging.who: Some people, because the list has stopped at 118 since 2016.
challenging.for: Each new element has been harder to make and has lasted a shorter time.
challenging.against: Laboratories in several countries are trying to make elements 119 and 120. Nothing known forbids them.

big_questions.q: By weight you are mostly oxygen. By number of atoms you are mostly hydrogen. Is one of these the real answer?
big_questions.hint: Imagine one lorry and three cycles on a road. If you count them, the cycles are more. If you weigh them, the lorry is more. Does one way of asking give the real answer?

big_questions.q: Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon. So what makes a thing what it is: its atoms or their arrangement?
big_questions.hint: The same bricks can be built into a wall or into a well. Would you say the bricks make the difference, or the way they are put together?

big_questions.q: Every hydrogen atom in your body is about 13.8 billion years old. So how old are you?
big_questions.hint: A new house can be built from very old bricks. Would you call the house old or new?

big_questions.q: Most elements are metals. Why might living bodies be built almost entirely from a few non-metals?
big_questions.hint: Think about what carbon can do that iron cannot: join into long chains.

big_questions.q: People once said the elements were earth, water, air and fire. Their list was wrong. Was their idea wrong?
big_questions.hint: They thought a few basic kinds make everything. Is that still what we think?

big_questions.q: Scientists made element 118 for about a thousandth of a second. Did that element exist before they made it?
big_questions.hint: Did the number 118 have a place in the list before anyone filled it?

story.title: The Black in the Lamp
story.note: Nila, Appu, Ammamma and the baby are made up. These things are real. In Kerala, many families make kanmashi at home for a baby's twenty-eighth day. They burn a cotton wick in oil under a plate or pot and collect the soot. Soot is mostly carbon. Coconut shells are burnt to charcoal for heavy box irons. Doctors today advise families not to put kajal or kanmashi in a baby's eyes.
text: On the day before the baby's twenty-eighth day, Ammamma lit the brass lamp in the middle of the afternoon, and that was how Nila knew it was a kanmashi day.

Kanmashi is the black that Ammamma made for every new baby in the family. She had made it for Nila nine years ago, and for Appu six years ago. Now there was a new cousin, asleep in the next room in a cloth cradle, and tomorrow she would get her name.

Nila and Appu sat on the cool red floor of the house in Thrissur and watched. Ammamma poured castor oil into the lamp. The oil was thick and pale yellow. She rolled a wick from clean white cotton and laid it in the oil. Then she stood three steel tumblers around the lamp and rested a small bronze plate on them, upside down, a hand's width above the wick.
"Now we wait," she said, and she lit the wick.

The flame was orange. The plate was the colour of dull gold. The oil was yellow and the wick was white. Appu counted the colours on his fingers. Then he lay on his stomach and looked up under the plate.
"Ammamma," he said, "something is making it black."
A soft black coat was growing on the bronze, exactly above the flame. It looked like velvet.
"That is the kanmashi," said Ammamma.
"But where is it coming from?" said Appu. "Nothing here is black."
Nila opened her mouth to answer and found that she did not know.
"I know," said Appu. "The fire is painting it. Fire paints things black. It painted my dosa this morning."
It was true that the edge of his dosa had burnt that morning. It was also true that he had refused to eat it.
"If fire paints things black," Nila said slowly, "then the lamp should be black."
They both looked at the lamp. It had stood in its own flame on every festival day for forty years. Around the wick it was brown with old oil, but under the oil it was brass, as yellow as ever.
"The lamp is strong," said Appu. "The fire cannot paint it."

"Salt is not strong," said Nila. She went to the kitchen and came back with a pinch of salt. She dropped a few grains on the hot rim of the lamp, beside the flame. They sat there. They did not turn brown. They did not turn black. They stayed as white as they had been in the jar.
Appu frowned. He did not like it when his ideas lost.

Nila was not looking at him. She was looking at the tip of the wick, where the white cotton went into the flame. The tip was black. She thought of the dosa edge. She thought of the coconut shells that the ironing woman at the corner burnt to charcoal for her heavy iron box. She thought of the time Amma forgot the payasam, and the sugar at the bottom of the pot turned into a black crust that took two days to scrub away.
"Dosa," she said. "Cotton. Coconut shell. Sugar. They all go black. Salt does not, and brass does not."
"So?" said Appu.

"So the fire is not putting the black in. The black must be inside them already, and the fire lets it out." She turned to her grandmother. "But the oil is yellow, Ammamma, and the wick is white. How can there be black inside?"
Ammamma did not answer at once. She turned the plate a little, so that a clean part of the bronze sat above the flame.
"Tell me where the cotton came from," she said.
"From a cotton plant."
"And the castor oil?"
"From castor seeds. From a plant."
"And the dosa, and the coconut shell, and the sugar?"
"Rice. A coconut tree. Sugarcane." Nila stopped. "They all grew. Every one of them grew."
"And the salt?"
"Salt comes from the sea. It never grew. And the lamp never grew."

Ammamma nodded. "Everything that grows is built out of the same black. A cotton plant builds white fluff from that black. A castor plant builds yellow oil. You cannot see the black, because it is joined up with other things. When the fire breaks them apart, the black is left over."
Appu had gone very quiet. He was looking through the doorway at the cradle, which was swinging a little.
"The baby is growing," he said.
"Yes," said Ammamma.
"So the black is in the baby." He looked at his own arm, and then at Nila. "And in me. And in her."
"In all three of you," said Ammamma. "And in me. A great deal of it."
"But I am brown," said Appu. "I am not black like the plate."
"Sugar is white," said Nila, "and you saw what was inside the sugar."
When the oil had burnt down, Ammamma let the plate cool. She scraped the soft black into a tiny silver box with the back of a spoon and worked one drop of ghee into it.
In the morning the house was full of aunts. The doctor had said nothing must go into the baby's eyes, so Ammamma put one small dot on the baby's cheek. Appu stood on a stool to see.
"Last year that dot was a cotton plant in a field," he told the nearest aunt. "It was inside the white, hiding."
The baby slept through everything, growing.
story.epiphany: Appu thought that fire paints things black. Nila saw that only things that once grew turn black, and salt and brass do not. The black is carbon. It is inside the white cotton and the yellow oil all the time, joined with other elements. Burning leaves it behind.
ask: Salt and brass sat next to the flame and did not turn black. What does that tell you about where the black comes from?
White cotton and yellow oil both left black soot. How can a black element be inside a white thing?
Name three things in your home that would leave black if they burnt, and one that would not.

games.title: Three of a Kind: an element set game
games.context: This is a card game with 24 element cards. You collect three cards that share something, such as three gases or three metals. You must say what they share.

setup.art: Twenty-four small cards in a shuffled pile, with five cards dealt face up in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them. Deal 5 cards to each player.

setup.art: A child laying three cards in a row on the table and speaking.
setup.caption: 2. On your turn, take one card. Lay down three cards that share something, and say what.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a short list of words: gases, metals, in the body.
setup.caption: 3. Write each shared thing on a list. Nobody may use it again.

Lead. Symbol Pb, from plumbum. Number 82. Metal. Solid. In your body: no.

rules: Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile. Two to four people can play.
On your turn, take the top card of the pile.
If three of your cards share something, lay them face up and say what they share. For example: 'All three are gases.'
The other players check the cards. If the set is true, write the shared thing on a list.
A shared thing on the list is used up. No player may use it again in this game.
After laying a set, take three new cards from the pile. Your turn then ends.
If you cannot make a set, put one card at the bottom of the pile. Your turn ends.
The first player to lay 2 sets wins. With two players, play to 3 sets.
Playing alone? Lay all 24 cards face up. Make as many sets of three as you can in 10 minutes. Each set needs a different shared thing. Eight sets is a perfect score.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards. Read three cards aloud together. Point to each of the six facts on a card.
flow.say: Each card gives an element's name, symbol and number. It also says its kind, its state, and whether your body needs it.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read three of them. Find the six facts.
flow.parent: State means solid, liquid or gas in an ordinary room. 'In your body' means the body needs that element.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three of a Kind. You get to know the six facts on each element card.

flow.do: Deal 5 cards each and play three turns each. Help with the first set if needed.
flow.say: Look for three cards that share something. They could share a kind, a state or something about their symbols. Say it aloud.
flow.kid: Take a card. Find three that share something. Say what they share.

ask.q: What different things can three element cards share?
good: All metals, or all non-metals.
All gases, or all solids.
All needed by the body.
All have a symbol from a Latin name.
All have a number under 10.

flow.parent: Easy sets such as 'all solids' get used up early. After that the players must look harder.
flow.context: In this step of Three of a Kind you play your first turns and lay your first sets.

flow.do: Play on until someone has laid 2 sets, or 3 sets with two players. Keep the list where all can see it.
flow.say: The easy sets are used up now. What else do your cards share? Look at the symbols and the numbers.
flow.kid: Keep playing. Each set needs a new shared thing.
flow.parent: Good late sets: symbols of one letter, symbols from Latin names, numbers above 40, elements not needed by the body.
flow.context: In this step of Three of a Kind you play to the end, and every set must share something new.

flow.do: Lay out all the metal cards in one row and all the non-metal cards in another. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Put the metals in one row and the non-metals in another. Now find the cards your body needs. Which row has more of them?
flow.kid: Make a metal row and a non-metal row. Which elements does your body need?

check.q: Which three elements are all non-metals that are in your body?
check.why: Oxygen, carbon and nitrogen are non-metals, and with hydrogen they make 96 parts in 100 of your weight. Iron, gold and silver are metals. If you chose helium, neon and mercury, check the cards: none of those is needed by the body.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three of a Kind. You sort the element cards into metals and non-metals.

games.title: Symbol Race: why is sodium Na?
games.context: This is a quick card game with 16 symbol cards. You see a symbol, such as Fe, and name the element. The back of each card gives the answer.

setup.caption: 2. One player holds up a card. The others name the element.

setup.caption: 3. Put each card on the 'know it' pile or the 'try again' pile.
