rules: One player is the reader. The reader holds up the top card so that the others see only the symbol.
The first player to say the element's name wins the card.
That player wins 1 more point by saying if it is a metal or a non-metal. The reader checks the back.
If nobody knows, the reader reads the back aloud. The card goes to the bottom of the pile.
Swap the reader after every four cards. The game ends when all 16 cards are won.
The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Look at each symbol, say the name, then turn the card over. Make a 'know it' pile and a 'try again' pile. Go through the 'try again' pile until it is empty.

flow.do: Make the 16 cards. Lay out the eight cards whose symbols come from Latin names: Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Hg and Pb.
flow.say: Eight of these symbols do not match the English name. They come from Latin, an old language that scientists once shared.
flow.kid: Make the cards. Find the eight symbols that look wrong.

ask.q: Why might scientists keep the old Latin symbols?
good: So everyone in every country uses the same letters.
Because old books and new books then agree.

flow.context: This is the first step of Symbol Race. You make the cards and look at the eight symbols that come from Latin names.

flow.do: Play through the pile once as a race, then once more. Keep score on paper.
flow.say: I will hold up a symbol. Say the element's name as fast as you can. Then say if it is a metal or a non-metal.
flow.kid: Look at the symbol. Say the name. Say metal or non-metal.
flow.context: In this step of Symbol Race you race to name each element from its symbol.

flow.do: Hold up Fe, then K, then Au, one at a time. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Fe is iron. Where have you seen the word 'ferrous'? K is potassium. Where have you seen NPK?
flow.kid: Name Fe, K and Au. Where have you seen these letters?

check.q: What does the symbol Na stand for?
check.why: Na is sodium, from its Latin name natrium. Nitrogen is N and neon is Ne. If you chose one of those, look again at the second letter.

flow.parent: 'Ferrous' is on iron tablets and syrup. NPK is on fertiliser bags: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
flow.context: This is the last step of Symbol Race. You link three Latin symbols to things at home.

experiments.title: The Black Test: which kitchen things hold carbon?
experiments.question: When eight kitchen things are heated on a tawa, which ones turn black? What do the ones that turn black have in common?
experiments.predict: Before the heating, guess for each of the eight things: will it turn black, or will it stay as it is? Sugar and salt look alike. Will they do the same thing? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use a small amount of each thing, no bigger than a 1 rupee coin. Put all eight on one sheet of foil on one tawa. Then they all get the same heat for the same time. Heat for 10 minutes on a medium flame. Only one thing differs from heap to heap: what the heap is made of.
results_table: Did it come from a living thing?

materials.item: an old tawa or a thick flat pan
aluminium foil, about 30 centimetres long, to cover the tawa
sugar, salt, raw rice and toor dal: a pinch of each, no bigger than a 1 rupee coin
a thumbnail-sized piece of bread, chapati or dosa
white cotton thread or a cotton wick, about 3 centimetres
a piece of plain paper, about 2 centimetres square
a steel safety pin or a steel paper clip
a steel spoon, a pencil, a sheet of white paper and a clock

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the heating. The child stays an arm's length from the stove. Open a window or switch on the kitchen fan, because the sugar smokes. Salt grains may crackle and jump. Let the foil cool for 10 minutes before anyone touches it.
experiments.record: Draw a table with eight rows, one for each thing. Write your guess, what it looked like after 10 minutes, and whether it came from a living thing.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up heats eight kitchen things on a foil-covered tawa. You find out which ones turn black, and what those ones share. The black is carbon.

setup.art: An old tawa covered with a sheet of foil, with eight numbers written on the foil in pencil around the edge.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the tawa with foil. Mark eight places with a pencil, well apart.

setup.art: Eight tiny heaps on the foil: sugar, salt, rice, dal, a piece of bread, a thread, a paper square and a safety pin.
setup.caption: 2. Put a small amount of each thing in its place. Write your guesses.

setup.art: A grown-up at a gas stove with the tawa on a medium flame, and a child watching from an arm's length away beside an open window.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up heats the tawa on a medium flame for 10 minutes. Watch from an arm's length.

setup.art: The cooled foil with six black heaps, a white heap of salt and a shiny safety pin, and a child rubbing a black crumb on white paper.
setup.caption: 4. Let the foil cool for 10 minutes. Then look, and rub the black on white paper.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: melted, brown, then a black crust

flow.do: Lay the eight things on a plate. Ask for a guess and a reason for each. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: A grown-up will heat these eight things for 10 minutes. Which will turn black, and which will stay the same? Sugar and salt look alike. Will they do the same thing? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the eight things. Which will turn black? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think sugar and salt will, or will not, behave the same?
good: They look the same, so they will do the same.
Sugar melts in a pan, so it may burn.
Salt is used in hot cooking and never burns.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say sugar and salt will do the same thing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Black Test. You guess which of eight kitchen things will turn black when heated.

flow.do: Cover the tawa with foil. Mark eight places with a pencil, about 5 centimetres apart. Put a small amount of each thing in its place.
flow.say: Each heap must be small, no bigger than a 1 rupee coin. Why should all eight go on the same tawa?
flow.kid: Put eight small heaps on the foil. Keep them well apart.
flow.parent: The same tawa gives every heap the same heat for the same time. Put the sugar near the edge, as it spreads when it melts.
flow.context: In this step of the Black Test you set out eight small heaps on a foil-covered tawa.

flow.do: Open a window. Heat the tawa on a medium flame for 10 minutes. Your child watches from an arm's length and says what changes. Then switch off the flame.
flow.say: Stay where you are and tell me what you see. Which heap changed first? What is the salt doing?
flow.kid: Stand back and watch. Which heap changes first? What does the salt do?
flow.parent: Sugar melts in a minute or two, bubbles, turns brown and then black. Bread, paper and thread darken next. Press the thread and paper flat with a spoon if they curl. Rice and dal are slowest and may only reach dark brown. If so, heat them for 5 minutes more. Salt may crackle.
flow.context: In this step of the Black Test a grown-up heats the eight heaps for 10 minutes while you watch.

flow.do: Wait 10 minutes for the foil to cool. Then your child fills in the table. They rub a black crumb of sugar or bread on white paper.
flow.say: Now it is cool. Write what each heap looks like. Rub a black crumb on the white paper. What does the mark remind you of?
flow.kid: Write what each heap looks like. Rub a black crumb on paper.

check.q: In the Black Test, which heap stayed white on the hot tawa?
check.why: Salt holds no carbon, so heat leaves nothing black behind. Sugar and rice hold carbon and turn dark. If you chose sugar, remember that looking alike does not mean being made of the same elements.

flow.parent: The black crumb leaves a grey-black mark, like a pencil or charcoal. All three are carbon.
flow.context: In this step of the Black Test you record which heaps turned black, and rub the black on paper.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Read them the note below only after they answer.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Look at the last column. What do the black ones share?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What do all the things that turned black have in common?
good: They all came from plants.
They all came from living things.
They all have carbon in them.

ask.q: Sugar is white. Where was the black before the heating?
good: Inside the sugar, joined to other elements.
It was hidden, and the heat left it behind.

flow.parent: The reason: everything that came from a living thing is made of compounds built around carbon. Heat breaks the compounds. Hydrogen and oxygen leave as water vapour and other gases, and black carbon stays. Salt and steel hold no carbon. Be honest about one limit. Chalk and cooking soda hold carbon joined tightly to oxygen, and they stay white. So black shows carbon, but white does not prove there is none.
flow.think: Your body grew from food like this rice and dal. What would the Black Test show about you?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Black Test. You say what the black heaps have in common.

experiments.title: Shine, Bend, Ring: which metal tests does pencil lead pass?
experiments.question: Pencil lead is carbon, a non-metal. If it goes through three tests for a metal, how many will it pass? How many will a burnt matchstick pass, which is also carbon?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will pencil lead pass none, one, two or all three of the metal tests? Will the burnt matchstick do the same as the pencil lead? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Do each test in the same way for every thing. Rub each thing five times with the same scrub pad. Bend each one with the same two fingers. Drop each one from the same height, one hand-width, onto the same upturned steel plate. Only the thing being tested changes.

materials.item: a steel spoon and a coin
a steel paper clip or a safety pin
aluminium foil: a piece as big as your palm, folded three times into a small pad
copper wire from an old electric cable, about 5 centimetres, with the plastic stripped off by a grown-up (leave it out if you have none)
pencil lead: a piece about 2 centimetres long from a broken pencil, with the wood cut away by a grown-up
a burnt wooden matchstick, or a small piece of charcoal
a dry green scrub pad, a steel plate, a torch or a phone light, and a sheet of newspaper

experiments.safety: A grown-up strips the wire, cuts the wood from the pencil lead, and burns and cools the matchstick. Wash your hands after handling the pencil lead and the burnt matchstick.
experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each thing and a column for each test. Write yes or no for shine and ring. Write 'bends' or 'snaps' for the bend test.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put metals and two forms of carbon through three tests: shine, bend and ring. You find out how many of the metal tests pencil lead passes.

setup.art: Seven small things in a row on newspaper: a steel spoon, a coin, a paper clip, a foil pad, a short copper wire, a piece of pencil lead and a burnt matchstick.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the things on newspaper. Guess how many tests the pencil lead will pass.

setup.art: A child rubbing a coin with a green scrub pad and shining a torch on it.
setup.caption: 2. Shine test. Rub each thing five times with the scrub pad. Look at it under a light.

setup.art: A child's fingers bending a paper clip, beside a pencil lead snapped in two.
setup.caption: 3. Bend test. Bend each thing gently with two fingers. Does it bend, or snap?

setup.art: A hand holding a coin one hand-width above an upturned steel plate.
setup.caption: 4. Ring test. Drop each thing from one hand-width onto an upturned steel plate. Listen.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: too stiff to bend by hand
too stiff to bend by hand

flow.do: Lay the things on newspaper. Say which element each one is made of. The steel is mostly iron. The foil is aluminium. The wire is copper. The pencil lead and the burnt matchstick are carbon. Then ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Pencil lead and this burnt matchstick are both carbon, a non-metal. We will give everything three metal tests. How many will the pencil lead pass? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pencil lead is carbon. How many metal tests will it pass? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the pencil lead will pass that many tests?
good: It is a non-metal, so it should pass none.
It looks a bit shiny, so it may pass one.
It is hard like metal, so it may ring.

flow.parent: Steel is mostly iron. Pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon, mixed with a little clay. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shine, Bend, Ring. You guess how many metal tests pencil lead will pass.

flow.do: Shine test. Your child rubs each thing five times with the dry scrub pad, then holds it under the light. They write yes or no.
flow.say: Rub five times, then hold it under the light. Does the rubbed part throw the light back? Look closely at the pencil lead.
flow.kid: Rub each thing five times. Hold it under the light. Does it shine?
flow.parent: Metals show a bright fresh surface. Pencil lead shows a grey shine too. The burnt matchstick stays dull black.
flow.context: In this step of Shine, Bend, Ring you rub each thing and look for a shine.

flow.do: Bend test. Your child bends each thing gently between two fingers, over the newspaper. They write 'bends' or 'snaps'.
flow.say: Bend each one gently. A metal bends and stays whole. What does the pencil lead do? What does the matchstick do?
flow.kid: Bend each thing gently. Does it bend, or does it snap?
flow.parent: The spoon and coin are too stiff to bend by hand. Write 'too stiff' for them. Nothing metal snaps.
flow.context: In this step of Shine, Bend, Ring you bend each thing to see whether it bends or snaps.

flow.do: Ring test. Turn a steel plate upside down on the floor. Your child drops each thing onto it from one hand-width and listens. They write yes or no.
flow.say: Drop each one from the same height. Listen for a ring that lasts. Which ones only tick or thud?
flow.kid: Drop each thing on the plate. Does it ring, or only tick?

check.q: In Shine, Bend, Ring, why is every thing dropped from the same height?
options: So only the thing itself changes
So the plate does not break
check.why: A higher drop makes a louder sound from anything. Keeping the height the same means a different sound comes from the thing itself. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test changes one thing at a time.

flow.parent: The foil pad hardly sounds, because it is thin, light and crumpled. Tap an aluminium vessel with a spoon to hear that aluminium does ring.
flow.context: In this step of Shine, Bend, Ring you drop each thing on a steel plate and listen for a ring.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Read them the note below only after they answer.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. How many tests did the pencil lead pass? Did the matchstick do the same?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Pencil lead and the burnt matchstick are both carbon. Why might they behave differently?
good: The atoms are arranged in different ways.
Pencil lead is in neat sheets and the burnt wood is jumbled.

ask.q: Is one test enough to decide that something is a metal?
good: No. Pencil lead shines but it is not a metal.
No. You need several tests that agree.

flow.parent: The reason: pencil lead passes the shine test and fails the other two. In graphite, carbon atoms sit in flat sheets. Some electrons are free to move along the sheets, as in a metal. So graphite shines and also carries electricity. The sheets slide apart easily, so it snaps and cannot ring. In burnt wood the carbon atoms are jumbled, so it is dull. Chemists call carbon a non-metal because of all its properties together.
flow.think: Diamond is also pure carbon. It is clear and very hard. What might be different about its atoms?
flow.context: This is the last step of Shine, Bend, Ring. You say how many metal tests pencil lead passed, and why.

activities.title: The Body Hundred Square: which elements are you made of?

materials.item: square-ruled paper from a maths notebook
colour pencils or crayons in seven colours
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Colour one hundred square for your body by weight, and a second one by number of atoms.

activities.record: Keep both squares. Under each, write the name of the element with the most squares.
activities.context: In this activity you colour two grids of 100 squares. The first shows the elements of your body by weight. The second shows them by number of atoms. The two grids look very different.

setup.art: A page of square-ruled paper with a box of 10 squares by 10 squares outlined in pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Outline a box of 10 squares by 10 squares. Guess which element will fill the most.

setup.art: The box coloured in bands: 65 blue, 18 black, 10 yellow, 3 green, 2 orange, 1 red and 1 purple, with a key beside it.
setup.caption: 2. By weight: colour 65 oxygen, 18 carbon, 10 hydrogen, 3 nitrogen, 2 calcium, 1 phosphorus, 1 for all the rest.

setup.art: A second box coloured 62 yellow, 24 blue, 12 black, 1 green and 1 purple.
setup.caption: 3. By number of atoms: colour 62 hydrogen, 24 oxygen, 12 carbon, 1 nitrogen, 1 for all the rest.

flow.do: Outline two boxes of 10 by 10 squares. Ask for the guess and the reason before giving any numbers.
flow.say: Your body is made of elements. Which one do you think makes up most of your weight? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which element is most of your weight? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why did you choose that element?
good: Calcium, because bones are heavy.
Iron, because blood has iron.
Carbon, because living things have carbon.
Oxygen, because we are mostly water.

flow.parent: Many children say calcium or iron. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Body Hundred Square. You guess which element makes up most of your body.

flow.do: Read out the weights. Your child colours the first box and makes a key. Use blue for oxygen, black for carbon and yellow for hydrogen.
flow.say: Out of 100 squares of weight, colour 65 for oxygen. Then 18 for carbon, 10 for hydrogen and 3 for nitrogen. Then 2 for calcium, 1 for phosphorus and 1 for everything else.
flow.kid: Colour 65 oxygen, 18 carbon, 10 hydrogen, 3 nitrogen. Then 2 calcium, 1 phosphorus, 1 the rest.

ask.q: Why might oxygen be so much of your weight?
good: We are mostly water, and water has oxygen.
Oxygen atoms are heavy.

flow.parent: The numbers are rounded so that they add up to 100. More than half of a body is water, and oxygen is eight ninths of the weight of water.
flow.context: In this step of the Body Hundred Square you colour the elements of your body by weight.

flow.do: Now read out the count of atoms. Your child colours the second box with the same colours.
flow.say: Now we count atoms one by one. Out of every 100 atoms in you, 62 are hydrogen. Then 24 are oxygen, 12 are carbon and 1 is nitrogen. The last 1 is everything else.
flow.kid: Colour 62 hydrogen, 24 oxygen, 12 carbon. Then 1 nitrogen and 1 the rest.
flow.context: In this step of the Body Hundred Square you colour the elements of your body by number of atoms.

flow.do: Put the two boxes side by side. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they see, and why the boxes differ.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you see, and why you think the two boxes differ. Which element wins in each box?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you see. Why do the boxes differ?

check.q: Hydrogen is 62 of every 100 atoms in you, but only 10 parts in 100 of your weight. Why?
options: Hydrogen leaks out of the body
check.why: A hydrogen atom is the lightest atom. An oxygen atom weighs about 16 times as much. So many hydrogen atoms add up to little weight. If you chose another answer, compare one oxygen atom with sixteen hydrogen atoms: they weigh the same.

flow.parent: Both boxes are correct. One answers 'which atoms carry most weight?' and the other answers 'which atoms are most common?'
flow.think: Someone asks what you are mostly made of. What would you ask them before you answer?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Body Hundred Square. You compare your body by weight with your body by number of atoms.

activities.title: Elements on the Label: how many of the 118 are in your home?

materials.item: packets and bottles with printed labels: iodised salt, toothpaste, a biscuit or health drink packet, a bottle of mineral water, a strip of vitamin or iron tablets, a packet of ORS, a battery
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Read the labels on eight things at home and list every element name you find.

activities.safety: A grown-up hands over any medicine strips and takes them back. Do not open them.
activities.record: Make a list with two columns: the element, and the label where you found it. Count the different elements at the end.
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels on packets and bottles at home. You list every element named on them, and count how many of the 118 you found.

setup.art: Eight packets and bottles from a kitchen and bathroom shelf, standing in a row on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Collect eight things with printed labels. Guess how many different elements you will find.

setup.art: A child's finger pointing at the word 'calcium' in the small print of a biscuit packet.
setup.caption: 2. Read the small print. Look for element names such as sodium, calcium, iron and zinc.

setup.art: A notebook list with two columns: element, and where it was found.
setup.caption: 3. Write each new element and where you found it. Count them at the end.

flow.do: Collect eight labelled things. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write the guess down.
flow.say: These labels name some of the elements inside. How many different elements do you think we will find? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many different elements will the labels name? Why do you think so?
flow.context: This is the first step of Elements on the Label. You guess how many elements the labels at home will name.

flow.do: Read each label together. Your child writes every element name and where it was found. Explain the changed endings.
flow.say: Look for sodium, potassium, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium and iodine. 'Fluoride' means fluorine, and 'chloride' means chlorine. The ending changes when the element is joined to another.
flow.kid: Read each label. Write every element name you find.

ask.q: The salt packet says 'iodised'. Which element was added, and why?
good: Iodine.
The body needs a little iodine, and many foods have too little.

flow.parent: Likely finds: sodium and iodine on salt, and fluoride on toothpaste. Food packets often name calcium and iron. Mineral water names magnesium and potassium. Tablets name zinc, and batteries name lithium or zinc. Most homes find 8 to 15.
flow.context: In this step of Elements on the Label you read eight labels and list the elements on them.

flow.do: Count the different elements. Ask which are metals. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Count your list. Most of these are metals, such as sodium and calcium. But nothing in the packets looks like metal. Why not?
flow.kid: Count your elements. Most are metals. Why can't you see any metal?

ask.q: Salt holds the metal sodium. Why does salt not look like a metal?
good: The sodium is joined to chlorine.
A compound looks different from its elements.

flow.parent: In salt, each sodium atom is joined to a chlorine atom. Joined in a compound, a metal does not shine, bend or ring. The same is true of the calcium in milk and the iron in blood.
flow.context: This is the last step of Elements on the Label. You count the elements you found and ask why the metals cannot be seen.

activities.title: The 118 Grid: how many of the elements are metals?

materials.item: square-ruled paper from a maths notebook
colour pencils in four colours: red, green, yellow and grey
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Number 118 squares, one for each element, and colour the non-metals, the metalloids and the metals.

activities.record: Keep the grid. Under it write how many squares are metals, metalloids and non-metals, and how many are too new to tell.
activities.context: In this activity you number 118 squares, one for each element. You colour the non-metals, the metalloids and the metals, and count each kind.

setup.art: A grid of squares in rows of ten, numbered 1 to 118 in pencil, with the last two squares of the twelfth row crossed out.
setup.caption: 1. Number 118 squares in rows of ten. Guess whether metals or non-metals are more.

setup.art: The same grid with seventeen squares coloured red and six coloured green.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the 17 non-metals red and the 6 metalloids green.

setup.art: The finished grid, mostly yellow, with the last ten squares grey.
setup.caption: 3. Colour 109 to 118 grey. Colour all the rest yellow for metals. Count each colour.

flow.do: Your child outlines 12 rows of 10 squares and crosses out the last two. They number the squares 1 to 118. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Each square is one element. Number 1 is hydrogen and number 118 is oganesson. Are more of the elements metals, or non-metals? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Number the squares 1 to 118. Are there more metals or non-metals? Why?
flow.parent: Many children guess non-metals, because air, water and their own bodies are non-metal.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 118 Grid. You number one square for each element and guess which kind is more common.

flow.do: Read out the non-metals: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 15, 16, 17, 18, 34, 35, 36, 53, 54 and 86. Your child colours them red. Then read out the metalloids: 5, 14, 32, 33, 51 and 52. They colour those green.
flow.say: Colour these seventeen squares red. They are the non-metals. Now colour these six green. They are the metalloids, such as silicon.
flow.kid: Colour the 17 non-metals red. Colour the 6 metalloids green.
flow.parent: Hydrogen is 1, carbon 6, nitrogen 7, oxygen 8, phosphorus 15 and sulfur 16. Silicon is 14.
flow.context: In this step of the 118 Grid you colour the 17 non-metals and the 6 metalloids.

flow.do: Your child colours squares 109 to 118 grey, then every square still white yellow. They count the yellow squares.
flow.say: Colour the last ten grey. Only a few atoms of each have been made, so nobody has tested them. Colour all the rest yellow. Those are metals. Count them.
flow.kid: Colour 109 to 118 grey. Colour the rest yellow. Count the yellow squares.

check.q: On the 118 Grid, how many of the first 108 elements are metals?
check.why: 108 take away 17 non-metals and 6 metalloids leaves 85 metals. If you chose 17, that is the number of non-metals. If you chose 6, that is the number of metalloids.

flow.context: In this step of the 118 Grid you colour the metals and count them.

flow.do: Your child puts a dot on squares 1, 6, 7, 8, 15 and 20. Ask them to say what they guessed, what they found, and what surprises them.
flow.say: Dot the six main elements of your body: 1, 6, 7, 8, 15 and 20. Say what you guessed and what you found. What colour are most of your dots?
flow.kid: Dot 1, 6, 7, 8, 15 and 20. What colour are most of your dots?

ask.q: Most squares are yellow, but five of your six dots are on red. What does that tell you?
good: Most elements are metals, but my body is mostly non-metals.
Living things are built mostly from non-metals, even though most elements are metals.

flow.parent: Calcium, number 20, is the only metal among the six. Chemists differ by one or two on the metalloid count, so some books give other totals.
flow.think: Where on your grid are the elements with the smallest numbers? Which colour are most of them?
flow.context: This is the last step of the 118 Grid. You mark the six main elements of your body on the grid.

projects.title: The Drying Potato: how much of a living thing is water?

materials.item: a medium potato
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a clothes hanger, two paper cups or small steel bowls, and thread, to make a balance
coins that are all of one value and one design
a steel plate and a sunny windowsill or a place under a fan

projects.safety: A grown-up slices the potato. Do not eat the dried slices.

schedule.what: Make the hanger balance and weigh the fresh potato slices in coins. Guess how many coins they will weigh when dry.
Turn the slices over again and check that they are getting hard.
Weigh the dry slices in coins and work out how much of the potato was water.

projects.record: Write the number of coins that balance the fresh slices on day 1. Write the number that balance the dry slices on day 4.
projects.context: In this four-day project you weigh thin slices of potato with a hanger balance and coins. You dry the slices and weigh them again. The weight that is lost was water, which is hydrogen and oxygen.

setup.art: A clothes hanger hanging from a door handle, with a paper cup hung by thread from each end.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a cup from each end of a hanger. Check that the hanger hangs level.

setup.art: Thin potato slices in one cup and a stack of coins in the other, with the hanger level.
setup.caption: 2. Put thin potato slices in one cup. Add coins to the other until the hanger is level. Count the coins.

setup.art: Potato slices spread out on a steel plate on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 3. Spread the slices on a plate in the sun or under a fan for three days. Turn them each day.

setup.art: Dry, curled potato slices in one cup and a few coins in the other.
setup.caption: 4. Weigh the dry slices in coins again.

flow.do: Day 1. Make the balance. Slice the potato as thin as a coin. Put slices in one cup until they balance 20 coins. Ask for the guess and the reason. Spread the slices on a plate.
flow.say: These slices weigh the same as 20 coins. We will dry them for three days. How many coins will they weigh then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The slices weigh 20 coins. How many when dry? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Use coins of one value and one design, because coins of different years can differ in weight. Thin slices dry faster and are less likely to spoil.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Drying Potato. You weigh fresh potato slices in coins and guess their dry weight.

flow.do: Days 2 and 3. Your child turns the slices over once a day and says how they have changed.
flow.say: Turn every slice over. How do they look and feel now? Where has the water gone?
flow.kid: Turn the slices over. How have they changed?
flow.wait: Do this on the second and third days
flow.parent: In damp weather the slices may stay soft or grow spots. Then a grown-up can dry fresh slices on a tawa on the lowest flame. This takes about 20 minutes, and the slices must be turned often.
flow.context: These are days 2 and 3 of the Drying Potato. You turn the potato slices as they dry.

flow.do: Day 4. Put the dry slices in one cup. Add coins to the other until the hanger is level. Ask your child to say what they guessed, what they found, and why.
flow.say: Count the coins that balance the dry slices. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why it happened. What was the lost weight?
flow.kid: Weigh the dry slices. Say what you guessed and what you found. Why?
flow.wait: Do this on the fourth day

ask.q: The slices went from 20 coins to about 4. What does that tell you about a potato?
good: About four fifths of it was water.
Most of a living thing is water.

ask.q: Water is hydrogen and oxygen. How does this help explain the Body Hundred Square?
good: A body is mostly water, so it is mostly oxygen by weight.
That is why oxygen had 65 squares.

flow.parent: Dry slices usually balance 4 or 5 coins, so about four fifths of the potato was water. A human body is about three fifths water. If your slices balance 6 or more coins, they are not fully dry.
flow.think: What are the 4 coins of dry potato made of? What would the Black Test show?
flow.context: This is day 4 of the Drying Potato. You weigh the dry potato slices and work out how much was water.

challenges.title: The Blindfold Sorter: tell metal from non-metal without looking
challenges.problem: A recycling centre must separate metal from everything else, quickly, without a person looking at each piece. Your problem is the same. Wear a blindfold and sort ten things into a metal bowl and a non-metal bowl. Design the tests you will use.
constraints: You may not look. Wear a blindfold or keep your eyes shut.
You may use at most two tests on each thing.
You must sort all ten things in 3 minutes.
You may use only your hands, your ears, a steel spoon and the floor.
Nothing may be broken or tasted.
materials: five metal things: a steel spoon, a coin, a key, a small steel bowl and a tight ball of aluminium foil
five non-metal things: a wooden spoon, a plastic lid, an eraser, a piece of chalk and a thick cardboard square
a cloth bag or a pillowcase
two large bowls and a clock or phone timer
general: Tap each thing with the steel spoon and listen. Most metals ring.
Hold each thing against your cheek or wrist. A metal feels cold, because it carries heat away from your skin.
Weigh each thing in your hand. Metal things are often heavy for their size.
creative: Drop each thing from one hand-width onto the floor and listen to the sound.
Squeeze each thing. A foil ball changes shape and keeps the new shape.
Use one quick test first, and a second test only when you are unsure.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own set of tests. It must sort all ten things in 3 minutes with no more than one mistake. Write the tests in order, and say which thing was hardest to sort and why.
challenges.context: In this challenge you sort ten things into metal and non-metal while blindfolded. You design the tests, using what metals share: they ring, they feel cold and they keep a new shape.

setup.art: Ten small household things beside a cloth bag, with two large empty bowls and a scarf.
setup.caption: 1. A helper puts five metal things and five non-metal things in a bag.

setup.art: A blindfolded child holding a key against her cheek, with one hand in the bag.
setup.caption: 2. Put on the blindfold. Take out one thing at a time and test it.

setup.art: Two bowls, one holding metal things and one holding non-metal things, and a phone timer showing three minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Put each thing in the metal bowl or the non-metal bowl. Stop at 3 minutes and check.

flow.do: Read the problem together. With eyes open, your child handles the ten things and says how metals feel and sound different.
flow.say: Before the blindfold, handle each thing. How does a metal feel on your cheek? How does it sound when tapped? Which tests could work without eyes?
flow.kid: Handle the ten things. How do metals feel and sound?

ask.q: Which properties of metals can you sense without looking?
good: They ring.
They feel cold.
They are heavy for their size.
Foil keeps its new shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Blindfold Sorter. You handle ten things and look for tests that work without seeing.

flow.do: Your child writes down two tests. A helper puts the things in the bag and starts the timer. Your child sorts blindfolded.
flow.say: Choose your two tests and write them down. Now put on the blindfold. You have 3 minutes. Go.
flow.kid: Choose two tests. Put on the blindfold. Sort all ten things.
flow.context: In this step of the Blindfold Sorter you sort ten things blindfolded with the tests you chose.

flow.do: Take off the blindfold. Count the mistakes together. Ask which thing fooled each test.
flow.say: Look in the bowls. How many are in the wrong bowl? Which thing fooled a test, and why?
flow.kid: Count your mistakes. Which thing fooled a test?
flow.parent: The foil ball often fools the tap test and the weight test, because it is light and does not ring. Chalk can feel cool.
flow.context: In this step of the Blindfold Sorter you count your mistakes and find what fooled each test.

flow.do: Your child changes one test and sorts again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Change one test and try again. Did you make fewer mistakes? Real recycling centres use machines for this. What might the machines sense?
flow.kid: Change one test. Sort again. Did you do better?

ask.q: A magnet picks up the spoon and the key but leaves the foil ball. Is a magnet a good test for metal?
good: No. It only finds iron and steel.
It is a test for iron, and some metals fail it.

flow.parent: Recycling centres use magnets to lift out iron and steel. Another machine uses a spinning magnet to push aluminium cans off the belt. Praise a clear account of what fooled a test as much as a perfect sort.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Blindfold Sorter. You improve the tests you chose and compare them with a recycling centre.

items.p: What is an element?
opts: A substance with one kind of atom
Any substance that is a solid
items.why: An element has only one kind of atom. Gold has only gold atoms. A mixture or a compound has more than one kind.

items.p: Scientists know ____ elements.
items.why: The elements are numbered 1 to 118. About 90 are found in nature, and people made the rest in laboratories.

items.p: Sugar is an element.
items.why: False. Sugar is a compound of three elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Heat can break it down, and an element cannot be broken down.

items.p: Match each symbol to its element.
items.why: O and C are the first letters of the English names. Fe comes from ferrum and Na from natrium, the Latin names.

items.p: Sort these elements: metal or non-metal?
items.why: Iron, copper and aluminium shine, bend and carry electricity. Oxygen and nitrogen are gases, and carbon is a brittle solid.

items.p: Which element makes up most of your body's weight?
items.why: Oxygen is 65 parts in every 100 of your weight, because your body is mostly water. Calcium is about 2 parts, and iron is far less than 1.

items.p: Put these body elements in order, from the most weight to the least.
items.why: In every 100 parts of weight, oxygen is 65, carbon is 18, hydrogen is 10 and nitrogen is 3.

items.p: Sugar turns black on a hot tawa. Salt stays white. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: Sugar is a compound that holds carbon. Heat drives off the hydrogen and oxygen as water vapour, and black carbon is left. Salt holds no carbon, so nothing black is left.
items.why: A strong answer says the carbon was inside the sugar before the heating. It also says that salt has no carbon.

items.p: Three of these are properties of most metals. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Metals shine, ring and bend. Crumbling when hit is being brittle, which is a property of solid non-metals such as charcoal.

items.p: Draw what a zoom into a grain of sugar might show. Use a different colour for each element.
items.a: Many small groups of joined balls in three colours, one each for carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The groups all look alike.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three kinds of atom joined together, and not three separate heaps. It has a key for the colours.
items.art: A sugar crystal with an empty zoom circle beside it.

items.p: What are you mostly made of?

views.says: Oxygen. It is 65 parts in every 100 of my weight.
Hydrogen. Out of every 100 atoms in me, 62 are hydrogen.
Carbon matters most. Every protein, fat and sugar in you is built on a frame of carbon atoms.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the Body Hundred Square. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. Oxygen is right by weight and hydrogen is right by number of atoms. The chemist is using a third meaning of 'mostly': what the body's compounds are built around.
items.why: Each view is true for one meaning of 'mostly'. A strong answer says which meaning it is using, and uses a number.

items.p: A body hundred square has 65 oxygen squares and 18 carbon squares. How many squares are left?
items.why: 65 and 18 make 83. 100 take away 83 leaves 17. Those 17 squares are hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and the rest.

items.p: Every metal is a solid at room temperature.
items.why: False. Mercury is a metal, and it is a liquid at room temperature.

items.p: Label the four largest bands on this body hundred square: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen.
items.why: The bands go in order of weight. Oxygen is by far the largest because the body is mostly water.
items.art: A hundred square in four large coloured bands of 65, 18, 10 and 3 squares and a small band of 4, each band with a blank label line.

items.p: The black left when food burns is mostly the element ____.
items.why: Food is made of compounds built around carbon. Strong heat drives off the other elements and leaves black carbon.

items.p: Pencil lead shines when rubbed but snaps when bent. What does this show?
opts: One test is not enough to decide
The bend test was done wrongly
Shine is not a real property
items.why: Pencil lead passes one metal test and fails others. Chemists sort an element by all its properties together.

items.p: Chalk stays white on a hot tawa. Does that prove chalk holds no carbon? Explain.
items.a: No. The Black Test shows carbon only when heat leaves it behind as a black solid. Chalk holds carbon joined tightly to oxygen, and a tawa is not hot enough to break that.
items.why: A strong answer sees the limit of the test. Black shows that carbon is there. White does not show that carbon is absent.

items.p: Sort these elements by their state at room temperature.
items.why: Most elements are solids. Only mercury and bromine are liquids. Eleven elements, such as oxygen and helium, are gases.

items.p: Match each element to its job in your body.
pairs: Needed by a gland in the neck
items.why: Each of these is a small part of the body's weight, but the body cannot work without it.

items.p: By number of atoms, hydrogen is the most common element in your body.
items.why: True. About 62 of every 100 atoms in you are hydrogen. Hydrogen atoms are so light that they are only 10 parts in 100 of your weight.

items.p: One particle of water has 2 hydrogen atoms. How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 particles of water?
items.why: 2 hydrogen atoms in each particle, times 5 particles, is 10 hydrogen atoms. There are also 5 oxygen atoms.

items.p: Fe is the symbol for ____.
items.why: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin name for iron.

items.p: Put these elements in order of atomic number, smallest first.
items.why: Hydrogen is 1, carbon is 6, oxygen is 8, iron is 26 and gold is 79.

items.p: Is pencil lead a metal?

views.who: A child who did the shine test
views.says: It shines, and it also carries electricity. So it is at least partly a metal.

views.who: A child who did the bend test
views.says: It snaps and it does not ring. It is carbon, so it is a non-metal.
It depends on how the atoms are arranged. In graphite some electrons move freely, as in a metal. In diamond none do.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Use a result from Shine, Bend, Ring. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. Chemists call carbon a non-metal because of all its properties together. The physicist's view explains why graphite still shines and carries electricity.
items.why: A strong answer uses at least one test result. It also sees that the answer depends on what 'metal' is taken to mean.

items.p: Salt holds the metal sodium. Why does salt not look like a metal?
opts: Its sodium is joined to chlorine
Its sodium has been used up
Sodium is not a real metal
items.why: In a compound the atoms are joined, and the compound has its own properties. The sodium is still there, and it can be taken out again.

items.p: Draw a strip of 10 squares to stand for the first 108 elements. Colour the share that are metals.
items.a: About 8 of the 10 squares are coloured. 85 of the first 108 elements are metals, which is close to 8 in every 10.
items.why: A strong drawing colours 8 squares and says how the number was reached.
items.art: An empty strip of ten squares.

items.p: Three of these are gases at room temperature. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Nitrogen, helium and oxygen are gases. Sulfur is a yellow, brittle solid.

items.p: Your blood holds iron. Explain why a magnet does not pull on your body.
items.a: A grown-up's body holds only 3 to 4 grams of iron, spread through all the blood. Each iron atom is joined into a compound. That compound is not magnetic the way a piece of iron is.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: the amount is tiny, and the iron is joined in a compound that behaves differently from iron metal.

items.p: Where were the carbon atoms in your body first made?
items.why: Stars build carbon from helium. Leaves take carbon from the air and join it into sugar, but they do not make the atoms.

items.p: Label each thing with the element it is mostly made of: kitchen foil, electric wire, pencil lead, a floating balloon.
items.why: Foil and wire are metals. Pencil lead is carbon, a non-metal solid. Helium is a non-metal gas lighter than air.
items.art: Four small pictures in a row, of a roll of foil, a cut cable, a pencil and a balloon on a string, each with a blank label line.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether a dry leaf holds carbon. Say what you would look for.
items.a: A grown-up heats a piece of the leaf on foil on a tawa. A pinch of salt goes next to it for comparison. If the leaf turns black and the salt stays white, the leaf holds carbon.
items.why: A strong answer includes something to compare with, and says what result would mean yes.

items.p: Were the old thinkers right that earth, water, air, fire and space are the elements?

views.who: A follower of the old list
views.says: Yes. Everything is solid, liquid, gas, heat or space. The five cover all that we meet.
No. Water splits into two gases, and air is a mixture. An element is something that cannot be split.
The list was wrong, but the idea was right. They saw that a few basic kinds make up everything.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The chemist is right about what an element is today. The historian points out that the search for a short list began with the old thinkers.
items.why: A strong answer separates the idea of a short list from the items on the list.

items.p: An atom has 79 protons. What must it be?
items.why: The number of protons decides the element. Every atom with 79 protons is gold, and no other element has 79.

items.p: A new element could be found with atomic number 6 and a half.
items.why: False. The atomic number counts protons, and protons come only in whole numbers. So there are no gaps between 6 and 7.

items.p: One oxygen atom weighs as much as 16 hydrogen atoms. How many hydrogen atoms balance 3 oxygen atoms?
items.why: 16 hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom, times 3, is 48 hydrogen atoms.

items.p: Sort these substances: element or compound?
items.why: Gold, oxygen and carbon each have one kind of atom. Water, salt and sugar are each two or three elements joined together.

items.p: Most elements are metals, but your body is mostly non-metals. Suggest one reason why.
items.a: Carbon atoms can join into long chains and rings, and metals cannot. With hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, these chains make water, fat, protein and sugar.
items.why: Nobody knows the full answer, so any reasoned idea counts. A strong answer names something non-metals can do that metals cannot.

items.p: Put these in the order they were made, earliest first.
items.why: Hydrogen formed soon after the universe began. Stars made carbon later. The Earth formed from matter that old stars scattered, and your body is built from the Earth's matter.

items.p: Deep inside Jupiter, hydrogen behaves as a metal. What is different there?
opts: How hard the atoms are squeezed
items.why: The atoms are still hydrogen, with 1 proton each. The enormous pressure frees their electrons to move, which is what makes a metal.

items.p: Match each fact to the property of metals that it shows.
pairs: Silver is beaten into leaf for sweets
items.why: People choose a metal for a job because of its properties. All four properties come from electrons that are free to move and atoms that can slide.

items.p: An element with some properties of a metal and some of a non-metal is called a ____.
items.why: Silicon is a metalloid. It shines like a metal, shatters like glass and carries electricity a little.

items.p: Draw two bars for the hydrogen in your body: its share of the weight, and its share of the atoms.
items.a: The weight bar reaches 10 out of 100. The atoms bar reaches 62 out of 100.
items.why: A strong drawing uses the same scale for both bars and labels each one.
items.art: Two empty bar outlines side by side on a scale from 0 to 100.

items.p: Three of these turn black when heated on a tawa. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Rice, cotton and paper came from plants and hold carbon. Salt holds no carbon and stays white.

items.p: Element 118 lasts about a thousandth of a second. Should it count as an element? Give a reason.
items.a: Chemists answer yes. Its atoms have 118 protons, and that is what makes it an element. A thoughtful no might say that nothing can be built from it or tested with it, because it lasts such a short time.
items.why: A strong answer uses what an element is: one kind of atom, fixed by its number of protons.

items.p: These five squares are numbered 1, 6, 8, 20 and 26. Write each element's symbol in its square.
items.why: All five are in your body. Fe is the only one of these whose symbol comes from a Latin name.
items.art: A row of five empty squares with the small numbers 1, 6, 8, 20 and 26 in their corners.

quiz.p: Which of these is an element?
quiz.why: Gold has only one kind of atom. Water, salt and sugar are compounds of two or three elements.

quiz.p: How many elements are known today?
quiz.why: 118 elements are known. Four was the old list of earth, water, air and fire. 92 is the number of uranium, the heaviest common element in nature.

quiz.p: What does the symbol K stand for?
quiz.why: K is potassium, from its Latin name kalium. Calcium is Ca, carbon is C and copper is Cu.

quiz.p: Which property do most metals share?
quiz.why: Metals carry electricity because some of their electrons move freely. Only a few metals, such as iron, stick to magnets.

quiz.p: Which of these is a non-metal?
quiz.why: Nitrogen is a non-metal gas. Sodium and calcium are metals, even though we never see them as metal in food.

quiz.p: Most of the 118 elements are which kind?
quiz.why: 85 of the first 108 elements are metals. Only 17 are non-metals, and 11 of those are gases.

quiz.p: Graphite is carbon, a non-metal, yet it carries electricity. What does this show?
opts: Some elements do not fit one side neatly
quiz.why: Graphite has one property of metals and lacks the others. The two groups are useful, but a few elements sit between them.

quiz.p: Which four elements make up 96 parts in every 100 of your weight?
quiz.why: Oxygen is 65, carbon 18, hydrogen 10 and nitrogen 3. All four are non-metals. Calcium and iron matter, but they weigh little.

quiz.p: Why is oxygen such a large part of your weight?
opts: You breathe it in all day
quiz.why: Water is most of your body, and oxygen is eight ninths of the weight of water. The oxygen you breathe in is a tiny amount at any moment.

quiz.p: Which element has the most atoms in your body?
quiz.why: About 62 of every 100 atoms in you are hydrogen. Oxygen wins by weight, because each oxygen atom is 16 times as heavy.

quiz.p: Bread turns black when it burns. What is the black?
opts: Carbon left behind from the bread
quiz.why: Bread is made of carbon compounds. Heat drives off the other elements and leaves carbon. Salt on the same tawa stays white, so the flame adds no black.

quiz.p: The elements in a living body are different from the elements in rocks and air.
quiz.why: False. Every element in a body is also found in rocks, air or sea. A body differs in how its elements are joined together.

videos.title: Sodium metal is soft and squishy
videos.why: To see a metal that is soft, light and quick to lose its shine. It widens the idea of what a metal is.
videos.check: Id, title and channel confirmed through YouTube's public lookup. Not watched from here: a parent should preview it.

videos.why: To see where the oxygen, carbon and calcium of the body were made.
videos.check: Id, title and channel confirmed through YouTube's public lookup. Not watched from here: a parent should preview it.

applications: Electric wires are made of copper or aluminium, because these metals carry electricity well and can be pulled into wire.
A little iodine is added to salt, because the body needs iodine and many foods hold too little.
Doctors measure the sodium, potassium, calcium and iron in a drop of blood to see how a body is working.
Recycling centres lift iron and steel out of mixed waste with magnets, and push aluminium out with a spinning magnet.
Computer chips are made of the metalloid silicon, because it carries electricity only a little and can be controlled.
Astronomers find which elements a star holds by studying the colours missing from its light.

open_questions.why_open: Laboratories are trying to make elements 119 and 120. Each new element is harder to make and breaks apart sooner. Nobody knows where the list must stop.

open_questions.q: Could some very heavy elements last a long time?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists predict an 'island' of heavy atoms that last for minutes or years. Nobody has reached it yet, so the idea is untested.

open_questions.q: Does life have to be built around carbon?
open_questions.why_open: All life on the Earth uses carbon. Silicon can also join to four atoms, but its chains are weaker. With only one example of life, nobody can be sure.

open_questions.q: Exactly which elements does a human body need?
open_questions.why_open: About 25 are agreed. For a few, such as chromium and boron, studies disagree, because the amounts are too small to test easily.

open_questions.q: Where was most of the universe's gold made?
open_questions.why_open: Colliding dead stars make gold, as astronomers saw in 2017. Whether such collisions are common enough to explain all the gold is still argued.

maths.problem: In the Body Hundred Square, oxygen is 65 parts in every 100 of your weight and carbon is 18. A child weighs 30 kilograms. About how many kilograms of the child are oxygen, and how many are carbon?
maths.answer: About 19 and a half kilograms of oxygen and about 5 and a half kilograms of carbon.
maths.explain: 65 parts in 100 of 30 kilograms is 30 times 65, divided by 100. That is 1,950 divided by 100, which is 19.5 kilograms. For carbon, 30 times 18 is 540, and 540 divided by 100 is 5.4 kilograms.
maths.context: In the Body Hundred Square you coloured 65 squares for oxygen and 18 for carbon, by weight. This problem turns the squares into kilograms.
maths.why_maths: Parts in a hundred turn a picture of squares into real amounts for a body of any weight.

maths.problem: A particle of water has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. A hydrogen atom weighs 1 unit and an oxygen atom weighs 16 units. What fraction of the atoms is hydrogen? What fraction of the weight is hydrogen?
maths.answer: Hydrogen is two thirds of the atoms, and one ninth of the weight.
maths.explain: There are 3 atoms and 2 are hydrogen, so two thirds. The weights are 1 + 1 + 16 = 18 units. Hydrogen is 2 of the 18 units. Divide both by 2 to get 1 ninth.
maths.context: In the Body Hundred Square, hydrogen filled 62 squares by number of atoms but only 10 by weight. Water shows why.
maths.why_maths: Two fractions of the same thing can differ. Working out both shows why counting and weighing give different answers.

maths.problem: In 100 atoms of your body, 62 are hydrogen, 24 are oxygen, 12 are carbon and 1 is nitrogen. They weigh 1, 16, 12 and 14 units each. Work out the weight of each group. Which group is heaviest, and is this what your first hundred square showed?
maths.answer: Hydrogen 62 units, oxygen 384, carbon 144, nitrogen 14. Oxygen is heaviest, as in the first square.
maths.explain: 62 times 1 is 62. 24 times 16 is 384. 12 times 12 is 144. 1 times 14 is 14. The total is 604 units. Oxygen is 384 of 604, which is a little under two thirds. The first square gave oxygen 65 squares in 100, which is also about two thirds.
maths.context: In the Body Hundred Square you coloured one square by weight and one by number of atoms. This problem checks whether the two squares agree with each other.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying each count by the weight of one atom joins the two squares. It shows that both describe the same body.

maths.problem: In the 118 Grid, 85 of the first 108 elements are metals. About how many in every 10 is that? If 20 elements were picked without looking, about how many would be metals?
maths.answer: About 8 in every 10. About 16 of the 20.
maths.explain: 85 out of 108 is close to 80 out of 100, which is 8 out of 10. For 20 elements, double it: about 16.
maths.context: In the 118 Grid you coloured the metals yellow and counted 85 among the first 108 elements.
maths.why_maths: A simple ratio such as 8 in 10 is easier to picture and to use than 85 in 108.

maths.problem: In the Black Test, sugar, rice, dal, bread, cotton and paper turned black. Salt and a steel pin did not. Which of these three would you expect to turn black: a dry leaf, a glass bead, a groundnut? Give the rule you used.
maths.answer: The dry leaf and the groundnut. The glass bead would not.
maths.explain: All six things that turned black came from living things, and both things that did not turn black never lived. The rule is: things made by living beings hold carbon that heat leaves behind. A leaf and a groundnut came from plants. Glass is made from sand.
maths.context: In the Black Test a grown-up heated eight kitchen things on a tawa, and you recorded which ones turned black.
maths.why_maths: Sorting results into two groups shows the pattern, and a pattern lets you predict a thing you have not tested.

maths.problem: In the Drying Potato, fresh slices balanced 20 coins and the dry slices balanced 4 coins. How many coins of weight were water? What fraction of the potato was water?
maths.answer: 16 coins of water. Four fifths of the potato.
maths.explain: 20 take away 4 is 16 coins. 16 out of 20 is the fraction. Divide both by 4 to get 4 out of 5.
maths.context: In the Drying Potato you weigh potato slices in coins before and after drying them. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare the potato with your own body, which is about three fifths water.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people start finding new elements, and how did they learn that the body is made of them? This card tells the true story of phosphorus.
how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, people called alchemists believed that ordinary matter could be turned into gold. Hennig Brand was a merchant in Hamburg in Germany. In 1669 he thought the secret might lie in urine, because urine is golden yellow. He collected many buckets of it. He let it stand for weeks, boiled it down to a paste, and heated the paste very strongly. No gold appeared. A white, waxy solid dripped out, and it glowed pale green in the dark. Brand had found phosphorus. He is said to be the first person known by name to discover an element. He kept his method secret and sold it. Robert Boyle in England worked out the method again in 1680. About a hundred years later, in Sweden, Johan Gahn found phosphorus in bones. Carl Scheele then made it from bone ash. In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier put phosphorus on his list of simple substances that nobody could break down. So a search for gold showed something else. The human body holds an element that no one had known, and that element can be taken out and held.
how_we_found_out.who: Hennig Brand in Hamburg. Later Robert Boyle in England, Johan Gahn and Carl Scheele in Sweden, and Antoine Lavoisier in France.
how_we_found_out.when: Brand found phosphorus in 1669. Boyle made it in 1680. Gahn found it in bones in 1769, and Scheele made it from bone ash in the 1770s. Lavoisier's list was printed in 1789.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That ordinary matter can be turned into gold. Brand also took the golden colour of urine as a sign of gold in it. His work gave no gold. It gave a new element. Later chemists showed that heating or mixing cannot change one element into another.

roots.context: In this unit you found the elements of your own body and counted them in two ways. Here we ask what those two counts say about you and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Body Hundred Square, you coloured 65 squares for oxygen when you counted by weight. When you counted atoms instead, 62 squares in 100 were hydrogen. Both counts are correct, because one oxygen atom weighs as much as 16 hydrogen atoms. So the question 'what are you mostly made of?' has two true answers, one for each way of counting.
deep_truth.habit: We expect a question such as 'what is this mostly made of?' to have only one answer. But the answer depends on whether you weigh the parts or count them. So how you ask the question changes the answer.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Body Hundred Square, the first box is mostly oxygen and the second box is mostly hydrogen. Now take the count of each kind of atom and multiply it by the weight of one atom of that kind. The second box then turns into the first box. So the two boxes describe the same body.

three.who_am_i: By weight you are mostly oxygen. By number of atoms you are mostly hydrogen, the simplest and oldest element.
three.what_is_life: In the Black Test, everything that came from a living plant left black carbon behind. A rice plant, a cotton plant and you are all built around the same element.
three.what_is_this_world: Stars, rocks, air and bodies are made from one list of 118 elements. Most of the list is metal, and most of you is non-metal.

roots.thread: Hydrogen is the simplest atom, with one proton. Stars pressed hydrogen together and built the heavier elements from it, step by step. Those elements joined into water, rock, rice and you. Many sages taught that the many things of the world come from one beginning. The science here says something close and plain. Every element in your body was built from the same simplest atom.

science.text: Every hydrogen atom in your body was made in the first minutes of the universe. That was about 13.8 billion years ago.
The carbon, oxygen and calcium in your body were made inside stars that died before the Sun formed.
Some philosophers, called panpsychists, think that even a single atom has a very simple kind of experience. Most scientists see no way yet to test this.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that a person is the elements and nothing more. Awareness arises when the elements come together in a body. They compared it to fermenting. Certain foods, mixed and left to stand, gain a new power to make people drunk. On this view, a list of your elements leaves nothing out. Many scientists today hold a view close to this one.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through, and they have not yet been tried at home. The Black Test (core) needs a tawa, foil and small amounts of eight kitchen things. A grown-up does all the heating. Sugar blackens within a few minutes and smokes, so keep each heap no bigger than a 1 rupee coin and open a window. Bread, paper and thread char next. Rice and dal are slowest and may only reach dark brown in 10 minutes, and the step says to heat them 5 minutes more. Salt may crackle and jump. Chalk and cooking soda hold carbon but stay white, and the parent note says so. The Body Hundred Square (core) needs only square-ruled paper and seven colours. Its numbers are rounded so that each box adds up to 100. Shine, Bend, Ring (core) needs a grown-up to cut the wood away from a pencil lead and to burn a matchstick. The ring test is weak for very small or thin pieces, so the foil pad makes almost no sound, and the step says how to hear aluminium ring. Pencil lead shows a grey shine, snaps and does not ring. The 118 Grid takes about 7 minutes of numbering before any colouring. Elements on the Label depends on the packets in the home, and most homes find 8 to 15 elements. The Drying Potato needs a sunny sill or a fan for three days. In damp weather the slices can spoil, and the step gives a tawa method. Coins of one value and one design must be used, and the balance is good only to about one coin. The Blindfold Sorter needs a helper. Three of a Kind was checked by hand: all 24 cards can be laid as eight sets with eight different shared things. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the 118 elements and their 2016 names, the body's shares by weight and by atoms, the Wöhler paper (volume corrected to 87), and the phosphorus story (Brand 1669, Boyle 1680, Gahn 1769 and Lavoisier 1789 stand). Softened: Brand as first named discoverer is now 'said to be', Scheele's date is now 'the 1770s', element 118's life is 'about a thousandth of a second', and the Weeks citation no longer gives a page. The metalloid count (6) is one common way of counting, as the unit says. The Upanishad and Sagan passages are paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
